newsitem.title: USA: Campaigning with Powell, Dole attacks Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Campaigning with Powell, Dole attacks Clinton.

text.p: Flanked by two of his most popular allies, running mate Jack Kemp and Gulf War hero Colin Powell, Bob Dole lashed out on Thursday at President Bill Clinton for allegedly sowing messages of fear and distrust.

Starting a two-day bus tour through the crucial state of Ohio, the Republican presidential candidate billed himself as a champion of "common sense conservatism" and said he is trustworthy but Clinton is not.
"Now, President Clinton's been talking a lot about a bridge to the future," he told a rally in Cincinnati. "What we really need is a bridge to the truth. A bridge to the truth."

"Remember President Reagan was the great communicator," he said. "President Clinton is the great exaggerator. He exaggerates everything that happens in America. He takes credit for everything. If that's the case, he can take the blame for drug use doubling" since he took office, Dole added.

He accused Clinton of using fear to disguise a lack of ideas, particularly by trying to frighten senior citizens and veterans by telling them that they would suffer under Dole's tax cuts. "Well, I believe the American people won't frighten so easily. What ought to scare you is four more years of Clinton and Gore," Dole said.

He had Kemp and Powell at his side for the first time since summer, opening up his two-day campaign bus tour through Ohio. Without a victory in the state, no 20th century Republican has ever won the presidency.
Powell has long been rumoured to be Dole's pick for secretary of state if the former Kansas senator scores an upset victory against Clinton.

Dole fuelled that speculation by telling reporters, "Colin Powell is going to be one of the stars of our new administration" but he was not specific. He said he hoped Powell would bring "excitement" to the campaign.

Despite suggestions that Powell would be a high-profile campaigner stumping energetically for Dole, this was only his second appearance at a campaign event since the Republican convention in August. He accompanied Dole to the Veterans of Foreign Wars convention in Louisville on Aug. 20.

Dole, Kemp and Powell rendezvoused in Cincinnati the morning after Kemp's debate with Vice President Al Gore in Florida. As expected, Dole said he thought Kemp was the clear winner in that matchup, although snapshot instant public opinion polls showed audiences thought Gore did better.
Dole credited Kemp with convincingly presenting his plans for tax cuts and economic growth and said public "support for our economic policy jumped eight points."

The Cincinnati rally was the start of a two-day bus trip, but Powell and Kemp were not scheduled to accompany Dole after the opening rally. Dole will have to compete for attention in Ohio on Thursday with Clinton, who was to visit Dayton.

Ohio has 21 electoral votes and many analysts regard it as "must win" territory for Dole. With the statehouse and most top local offices firmly in Republican hands, Dole should have some help here but polls show he is lagging far behind Clinton, who narrowly carried Ohio in 1992.
